Here is a verse-by-verse commentary on Numbers 28 drawn from the sources I could reach within the search and fetch limits.

---

## Numbers 28 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview

Numbers 28–29 form a unit: a comprehensive calendar of the minimum public sacrifices the priests were to offer for the nation throughout the year, arranged by frequency — daily, weekly (Sabbath), monthly (new moon), and then the annual feasts in chronological order (spring feasts in ch. 28, fall feasts in ch. 29). The offerings are cumulative: each later offering is added to, never replacing, the daily one. All the older commentators agree the passage was given to the new generation about to enter Canaan, since the sacrificial system had been largely in abeyance during the wilderness wanderings and needed fresh promulgation (Gill, Ellicott, Calvin). Constable calls this “another step in preparing to enter Canaan” in that “the real key to successful conquest … was continual fellowship with God.”

---

### v. 1: “Then the LORD said to Moses,”

**Gill** notes the context: the census had been taken, land-division orders given, and now “it was thought proper by the Lord to renew, or to put in mind of, the laws concerning sacrifices” — it had been 38 years since they were first made, a new generation had arisen, and Moses was about to die.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

**Ellicott** agrees: “The sacrificial laws had been to a great extent in abeyance during the wanderings … It was needful, therefore, that before the entrance into the land of Canaan those laws should be promulgated afresh.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/28.htm

**Pulpit Commentary** is more cautious on dating, saying it is “impossible to say with any assurance” whether this was given shortly before Moses’ death or compiled later by an editor from scattered Mosaic regulations. But it affirms “the system itself was of Divine origin, and dated in substance from the days of Moses.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

---

### v. 2: “Command the Israelites … present to Me at its appointed time the food for My offerings by fire, as a pleasing aroma to Me.”

**Enduring Word** (David Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic) highlights the possessive language: “My offering, My food … The sacrifices God told Israel to make belonged to Him. They were to be made according to His command, and not improvised.” He quotes F.B. Meyer: “We often speak of ourselves as hungering for God. Do we sufficiently realize that He hungers for our love, our whole-hearted devotion, our fellowship with Him?”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-28/

**Gill** says the Hebrew *korban* (“offering”) and *lechem* (“bread”) indicate the sacrifices symbolically served as God’s food — “the provisions of his house, of which there were all sorts … flesh, bread, and wine.” He adds that this was “not merely as commands and duties … but as tokens of the divine favour to them, that notwithstanding all their rebellions … sacrifices for sin were ordered, continued, and accepted.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

**Precept Austin** stresses the repeated “MY … MY … MY … ME”: “God is making it clear that these offerings are for HIM!” The appointed times speak of a rhythm that kept Israel continually reminded of their need for atonement — all pointing to “the ultimate sacrifice of the Lamb of God Who takes away the sins of the world (Jn 1:29).”
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-28-commentary

**Ellicott** notes that the word *korban* “is a general term for an oblation” and that *lehem* (bread) “may be used to denote food generally, the sacrificial offerings being symbolically regarded as the Lord’s food” (cf. Lev 3:11, 16; Mal 3:7).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/28.htm

**Gaebelein** (dispensational/Brethren) emphasises a Christological reading: “Needless to say that all speaks of Christ. He is seen in all the offerings … In Christ God has found His delight … The heart of God feeds, humanly speaking, upon Christ.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/numbers-28.html

---

### v. 3: “two unblemished year-old male lambs … as a regular burnt offering each day”

**Enduring Word**: Each day began and ended with “a statement of the need for atonement by sacrifice and expression of surrender and devotion to the LORD.” The daily offering is the foundation for everything else.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-28/

**Ellicott**: “The morning and evening lamb offered as ‘a continual burnt offering’ afforded a striking type of the Lamb of God offered once for all (Hebrews 7:3; Hebrews 10:12; Hebrews 10:14).”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/28.htm

**Gill**: The lambs were “without spot” — a qualification not expressed in the original Exodus 29 ordinance but now explicit. They are “typical of Christ, the Lamb of God, without spot and blemish.” The offering was “continual” — “offered every day … without any intermission, on any account whatever … until the Messiah came, who put an end to it by the sacrifice of himself.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

**Pulpit Commentary**: “The daily offering … formed the foundation of the whole sacrificial system. Whatever else was offered was in addition to it, not in lieu of it. The sabbath and festival use of the Jews was developed out of the ferial use, and rested upon it.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

---

### v. 4: “Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight”

**Enduring Word** connects this to the psalmists’ practice (Ps 5:3; 88:13; 141:2; 55:17) and notes Jesus died “at the time of the evening sacrifice.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-28/

**Gill** cites the Targum of Jonathan: the morning lamb made “atonement for the sins of the night,” the evening lamb “for the sins of the day.” Both prefigured Christ who “continually, every day, morning and night, and every moment, takes away the sins of his people.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

**Ellicott**: “At even” is literally “between the two evenings” (cf. Ex 12:6).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/28.htm

---

### v. 5: “a tenth of an ephah of fine flour … mixed with a quarter hin of oil from pressed olives”

**Enduring Word**: The grain offering (fine flour mixed with oil) and later the drink offering accompanied each lamb. “The flour is as important as the animal; the wine is as significant as the oil. The sacrifices will not be appropriate if any element is not acceptable or if any element is not in the right proportion” (quoting Allen).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-28/

**Ellicott**: “Beaten oil” refers back to Exodus 27:20 — the purest oil, obtained by pounding rather than crushing, used for the lampstand and here for the grain offering.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/28.htm

---

### v. 6: “a regular burnt offering established at Mount Sinai … a pleasing aroma”

**Gill**: The phrase “ordained in Mount Sinai” indicates this was not new but a republication of what was given long before. He notes an interpretive question from Aben Ezra: does “made” (or “offered”) at Sinai imply they ceased offering it afterwards in the wilderness? But Gill doubts this, noting the altar fire was to burn continually.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

**Precept Austin**: “Burnt offering” (*‘olah*) occurs 14 times in this chapter. The word means “what ascends” in smoke and emphasises that the offering is wholly consumed — nothing kept back — distinct from offerings where portions were eaten.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-28-commentary

---

### v. 7: “The drink offering … a quarter hin. Pour out the offering of fermented drink to the LORD in the sanctuary area.”

**Pulpit Commentary** makes a distinctive observation: the Hebrew word for the drink is *shecar* (“strong drink”), not the usual *yayin* (wine). *Shecar* normally denotes an intoxicating drink other than grape wine (as in Lev 10:9, Num 6:3). The Pulpit suggests “the difficulty of procuring wine in the wilderness had caused the coarser and commoner liquor to be substituted for it” and adds that its retention in the text “may be accepted as evidence of the wilderness-origin of this particular ordinance.” The quantity — about a quart per lamb — “was very considerable.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

**Ellicott**: *Shecar* “denotes any kind of intoxicating drink, whether made from grapes, honey, or grain.” The drink offering was poured out at the altar of burnt sacrifice (inferred from Ex 30:9, which forbids drink offerings on the incense altar).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/28.htm

**Gill**: The Targums render it “old wine,” but the point is it was “the strongest, best, and choicest that could be got … all which was typical of the sufferings, sacrifice, and bloodshed of Christ.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

---

### v. 8: “Offer the second lamb at twilight, with the same grain offering and drink offering as in the morning.”

**Gill**: The evening offering was identical — same lamb, same grain, same drink offering. The repetition of “a sweet savour unto the Lord” is “to encourage the people to offer it, and to show how very acceptable it was.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

---

### vv. 9–10: “On the Sabbath day, present two unblemished year-old male lambs … This is the burnt offering for every Sabbath, in addition to the regular burnt offering.”

**Ellicott**: “The Sabbath offering which was to be added to the daily sacrifice is here enjoined for the first time.” The Sabbath law itself was given in Ex 20:8–11 and Lev 23:3, but the specific sacrifice is new here.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/28.htm

**Pulpit Commentary**: The Sabbath offering was slain “immediately after the morning sacrifice of the day.” Verse 10 literally reads “the sabbath burnt offering for its sabbath” — meaning each Sabbath’s sacrifice was for that Sabbath alone; it could not be deferred or made up later.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

**Enduring Word**: The Sabbath doubled the daily offering (two lambs instead of one morning lamb). “The Sabbath offering was in addition to the daily morning and evening offerings.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-28/

**Calvin** (Reformed): “What was omitted in the former passage is here supplied, i.e., that on the Sabbath the continual sacrifice was to be doubled … it was reasonable that, as the seventh day was peculiarly dedicated to God, it should be exalted above other days by some extraordinary and distinctive mark.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-28.html

---

### vv. 11–15: The Monthly (New Moon) Offering

**v. 11**: “two young bulls, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old, all unblemished”

**Pulpit Commentary**: The new-moon offering is “here enjoined for the first time” (the festival was only incidentally mentioned in Num 10:10). Unlike the Sabbath, the new-moon “was a nature-festival, observed more or less by all nations” — it did not need to be instituted, only “regulated and sanctified in order that it might not lend itself to idolatry.” It became “to the month exactly what the sabbath was to the week — a day of rest and of worship” (cf. 1 Sam 20:5; 2 Kgs 4:23; Isa 66:23; Amos 8:5).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

**Enduring Word**: The new moon was “an opportunity for family worship … and all trading ceased (Amos 8:5).” Quoting Poole: the goat was offered “unto the LORD, not unto the moon, to which the Gentiles offered it.” Later Israel corrupted these festivals: “Your New Moons and your appointed feasts My soul hates” (Isa 1:14).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-28/

**Calvin**: The goat sin offering was added “in order that every month they should present themselves as guilty before God to deprecate His wrath.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/numbers-28.html

**v. 14**: drink offerings tiered — half a hin per bull, a third per ram, a quarter per lamb.

**Gill**: The quantities match Num 15:4–5, where the oil for the grain offerings was also specified: half a hin per bullock, a third per ram, a quarter per lamb.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

**v. 15**: “one male goat … as a sin offering … in addition to the regular burnt offering”

**Pulpit Commentary**: The goat (*sa‘ir*, “hairy one”) was “probably offered first in order, according to the usual analogy of such sacrifices (Ex 29:10–14).” The Pulpit also clarifies this sin offering was part of the routine cycle and did not supersede the occasional sin offering of Num 15:24ff.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

**Enduring Word** notes the principle of accumulation: daily + weekly + monthly all possible on the same day. “This was a dramatic declaration of the principle that as time goes on, our need becomes greater, not less.” Quoting G. Campbell Morgan: “An increase in the number of sacrifices, and a growing importance in the religious rites, is marked in the growth of time divisions.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-28/

---

### vv. 16–25: Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread

**v. 16**: “The fourteenth day of the first month is the LORD’s Passover.”

**Ellicott**: “The observance of the Passover had been in abeyance for thirty-eight years. The law is now promulgated afresh.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/28.htm

**Gill**: The month is Nisan/Abib, made the first month at the Exodus (Ex 12:2). Passover commemorates the Lord’s passing over Israelite houses in Egypt.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

**Enduring Word** quotes Watson: “The Passover, the first great feast, a sacrament rather, is merely mentioned in this portion of Numbers. It was chiefly a domestic celebration — not priestly — and had a most impressive significance, of which the eating of the lamb with bitter herbs was the symbol.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-28/

**v. 17**: “On the fifteenth day … seven days unleavened bread is to be eaten.”

**Pulpit Commentary**: The fourteenth (Passover proper) “was not a feast, but a fast ending with the sacred meal of the evening. Only the ordinary daily sacrifice was offered on this day.” The feast began on the fifteenth.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

**v. 18**: “sacred assembly … you must not do any regular work.”

**Gill**: The first day is a holy convocation with no servile work “except by preparing food to eat” (cf. Ex 12:16).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

**vv. 19–22**: The daily festival sacrifice: two bulls, one ram, seven lambs, with grain offerings and one goat for a sin offering.

**Pulpit Commentary**: This offering “had not been prescribed before, and almost certainly not observed at the one passover kept in the wilderness (Num 9:5).”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

**v. 23**: “present these in addition to the regular morning burnt offering.”

**Pulpit Commentary**: “i.e., in addition to, and immediately after, the usual morning sacrifice.” It stresses the cumulative principle: on the Sabbath of Passover (John 19:31), the sacrifices would include (1) the daily, (2) the Sabbath, and (3) the Feast of Unleavened Bread — “two bullocks, one ram, eleven lambs, with their meat offerings and drink offerings.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

---

### vv. 26–31: The Feast of Weeks (Pentecost / Firstfruits)

**v. 26**: “On the day of firstfruits, when you present an offering of new grain … you are to hold a sacred assembly.”

**Gill**: This is Pentecost, 50 days from the wave sheaf offering. The “new meat offering” was the two wave loaves of fine flour baked with leaven (Lev 23:15–17).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

**Enduring Word**: “The Feast of Weeks, also called the day of firstfruits of the wheat harvest (Exodus 34:22). … The highlight of the festival was the priest’s waving of the two bread loaves of new grain and the two lambs of the fellowship offering (Leviticus 23:15–21).” Even this joyful harvest feast includes a sin offering — “a constant reminder that gratitude and confession belong together.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-28/

**vv. 27–29**: burnt offering of two bulls, one ram, seven lambs, with tiered grain offerings.

**Ellicott** notes a discrepancy with Leviticus 23:18, where the animal sacrifices are “one young bullock, two rams, and seven lambs.” The Mishnah (Menach. iv. 2) resolved this by treating the Numbers list as additional sacrifices of the day, not the same ones. Josephus thought three bullocks, two [three] rams, and fourteen sheep were offered (Antt. iii. 10, § 6).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/28.htm

**Pulpit Commentary** adds: “The festal sacrifice here prescribed is exactly the same as for the days of Mattsoth and for the feast of the new moon. It is not the same as that prescribed for the same day in Leviticus 23, and it is difficult to determine whether it was meant to supersede the previous ordinance, or to be distinct and additional.” The Pulpit leans towards the two lists being independent — “throughout this section no sacrifices are mentioned save such as formed a part of the system which is here for the first time elaborated.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

**v. 30**: “Include one male goat to make atonement for you.”

**Gill**: “For notwithstanding all their services and sacrifices, and though this day was an holy convocation, yet there was need of a sin offering to expiate their guilt, typical of Christ, who takes away the sins of our holy things as well as all other sins.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/28.htm

**v. 31**: “Offer them with their drink offerings in addition to the regular burnt offering and its grain offering. The animals must be unblemished.”

**Enduring Word**, citing Adam Clarke: “This is to be understood as applying, not only to the animals, but also to the flour, wine, and oil; every thing must be perfect in its kind.”
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-28/

---

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The sources I was able to access within the search and fetch limits did not reveal pronounced *doctrinal disagreements* among Protestant traditions specifically on Numbers 28. This is largely because the chapter is ritual/calendar legislation. However, several distinct interpretive emphases emerged:

**Christological typology (broadly shared, but stressed differently):**

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Strong practical application — morning and evening offerings model daily devotional rhythms; the “relentless” priestly work contrasts with Christ’s finished work where “He sat down” (Heb 10:11–12). Emphasises that God “hungers for our love” (Meyer).
- **Reformed (Calvin):** Stresses God’s sovereignty in prescribing worship: the Sabbath offering “exalts” the day “above other days by some extraordinary and distinctive mark.” The sin offering reminds that “every month they should present themselves as guilty before God.”
- **Baptist (Gill):** Emphasises the typical/prophetic relationship to Christ throughout — each lamb, the flour, the wine all point to Christ’s person and work. Gill also engages with rabbinic sources (Targums, Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Maimonides) more than any other commentator here.
- **Dispensational/Brethren (Gaebelein):** Reads the offerings Christologically from the divine side: these are “Jehovah’s portion which he is to receive in the worship of His people … The heart of God feeds, humanly speaking, upon Christ.”
- **Evangelical (Constable, Allen):** Stresses that all sacrifices “have their ultimate meaning in the death the Savior died. Apart from his death, these sacrifices were just the killing of animals.” After Christ’s death, such sacrifices “are redundant — indeed, offensive.”

**On the drink offering as *shecar* (“strong drink”):**

The Pulpit Commentary’s suggestion that *shecar* (not wine) reflects a wilderness-origin (wine being scarce) is a more critical/liberal-leaning observation. Gill and the Targums harmonise it by rendering it “old wine.” This is a textual rather than denominational difference.

---

## Other Views

### Modern / Critical Scholarship

**Pulpit Commentary** (late 19th c., moderately critical): Raises the question whether Numbers 28–29 was “really given to Moses shortly before his death, or whether it was ever given in this connected and completed form.” It allows that a “subsequent editor” may have compiled scattered Mosaic regulations. Yet it affirms “the system itself was of Divine origin, and dated in substance from the days of Moses.”
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/28.htm

**Ellicott** (Anglican, 19th c.): Notes that the details of Passover sacrifices “are not found in Leviticus 23,” which “may be adduced in proof of the prospective character of much of the Levitical legislation” — i.e., some laws were given with future settlement in view, supporting Mosaic authorship.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/28.htm

**The Expositor’s Bible Commentary** notes that “the legislation of chapters 28–30 appears to belong to a time of developed ritual and organised society. Parallel passages in Exodus and Leviticus … are by no means so full in their details, nor do they even mention some of the sacrifices here made statutory.”
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/numbers-28.html

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

**No results were returned** from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within my search limits for Numbers 28 specifically. I was unable to fetch or locate distinctively Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this chapter.

---

## Summary of Key Themes

1. **God’s ownership**: The repeated “My offering, My food” signals that worship is on God’s terms, not human invention.
2. **Cumulative need**: Sacrifices pile up — daily, Sabbath, new moon, annual feasts — never cancelling but always adding, teaching that “as time goes on, our need becomes greater, not less” for atonement.
3. **All pointing to Christ**: Lambs without blemish, wholly consumed burnt offerings, poured-out drink offerings — every element typifies the Lamb of God and His finished work.
4. **Rhythm of devotion**: Morning and evening framing of each day with sacrifice models a life oriented around God at the boundaries of time.
